prompt: Which question does a review answer?
hint: Two people can write the same fix differently.

choices.text: Is this how I would have written it?
choices.why: Then every change would be rewritten in the reviewer's style.

choices.text: Did the author work hard enough?
choices.why: A review reads the change, not the person.

choices.text: Does it follow every rule of the style guide?
choices.why: Machines check most of that, and it comes last.

choices.text: Is this good enough to merge?
choices.why: Right. A change can pass while you would still do it differently.

prompt: What does review give a team? Choose all that apply.
hint: One of them matters most when somebody is on holiday.

choices.text: A second chance to catch a mistake
choices.why: Yes. The reviewer reads what is there, not what was meant.

choices.text: A second person who knows the code
choices.why: Yes. Somebody else has read it before it breaks.

choices.text: A guarantee that the code has no bugs
choices.why: It lowers the odds; nothing guarantees that.

choices.text: A record of who is the better developer
choices.why: Review is not a ranking.

prompt: Put the questions a reviewer asks in the order the lesson reads them.
hint: A problem in the first makes the last irrelevant.
items: Does it do what the ticket asked?
Can the next person understand it?
Is it consistent with the rest?
trap: Polishing names first spends the review on a change that may solve the wrong problem.

prompt: A pull request has inconsistent indentation. Who should catch that?
hint: It is the same fix every time.

choices.text: An automatic check or formatter
choices.why: Right. It catches it every time and frees the reviewer.

choices.text: The most senior reviewer
choices.why: Their attention is worth more elsewhere.

choices.text: The customer, after the release
choices.why: Customers never see indentation.

choices.text: Nobody; it does not matter
choices.why: It matters a little, and a machine can handle it.

prompt: Why does Ana fetch Bruno's branch instead of only reading the diff on the website?

choices.text: The website hides some lines
choices.why: It shows the same diff.

choices.text: She needs it to approve
choices.why: Approving is a button on the website.

choices.text: To merge it herself
choices.why: Merging happens on the pull request.

choices.text: To run it, not only read it
choices.why: Right. Pressing Order with an empty field showed the bug.

prompt: Why does the lesson use git diff main... with three dots?
hint: Where did the branch leave main?

choices.text: Three dots include uncommitted changes
choices.why: Neither form looks at the working directory here.

choices.text: To see only the branch's own work
choices.why: Right. It compares with where the branch left main.

choices.text: Two dots are not valid with diff
choices.why: They are valid, and would also show main's new commits reversed.

choices.text: Three dots show the commit messages
choices.why: diff shows lines; log shows messages.

prompt: git diff --stat shows that a pull request about ordering changed style.css. What should a reviewer make of that?
hint: The shape can raise a question before any line is read.

choices.text: Check the style change belongs
choices.why: Right. Here the heading colour did not.

choices.text: Nothing; stat only counts lines
choices.why: The counts say which files, and that is information.

choices.text: Reject the pull request
choices.why: A form may need styling; look before deciding.

choices.text: Run the formatter on style.css
choices.why: Formatting was not the issue.

prompt: You are asked to review a pull request of two thousand lines. What is the honest response?
hint: A review that skims and approves helps nobody.

choices.text: Approve it; the author knows the code
choices.why: Then the review caught nothing and said it did.

choices.text: Ask for it split, or a walk through
choices.why: Right. Say you cannot review it well as it is.

choices.text: Comment only on the first file
choices.why: The rest merges unread.

choices.text: Ignore it until it is smaller
choices.why: Silence helps nobody; say what you need.

prompt: Match each comment on #31 to its kind.
hint: How much does each one need to change before the merge?

pairs.left: Place order says more than Order

prompt: Which comment will help Bruno most?
hint: Can he check it and act on it?

choices.text: This is wrong.
choices.why: He cannot tell what is wrong or how much it matters.

choices.text: You forgot the validation again.
choices.why: Aimed at the person, and again adds blame.

choices.text: Empty submits; add required?
choices.why: Right. What happens, and a fix he can take or not.

choices.text: I would redo this form from scratch.
choices.why: It gives no reason and no direction.

prompt: What makes the blocking comment on #31 useful? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four things; one option is not among them.

choices.text: It says what happens
choices.why: Yes. Bruno can check it in seconds.

choices.text: It says why that matters
choices.why: Yes. An order with no time cannot be fulfilled.

choices.text: It suggests a fix
choices.why: Yes. He may take it or do it differently.

choices.text: It names who made the mistake
choices.why: It is about the line, not the person.

choices.text: It says how serious it is
choices.why: Yes. blocking: tells him it must change.

prompt: Why is "Why didn't you just use a list?" a poor review comment?

choices.text: Lists are always worse
choices.why: Lists are fine; the comment's shape is the problem.

choices.text: A demand posing as a question
choices.why: Right. The author has to guess which it is.

choices.text: Questions are not allowed in reviews
choices.why: Real questions are welcome.

choices.text: It is too short
choices.why: Length is not the issue.

prompt: Why say what is good in a change, specifically?

choices.text: To make the blocking comment feel optional
choices.why: Blocking stays blocking.

choices.text: Because every review needs a compliment
choices.why: Only when it is true and specific.

choices.text: To get a better review back
choices.why: Review is not a trade.

choices.text: It teaches, and shows you read it
choices.why: Right. A specific compliment is information.

prompt: Before posting a comment, what question separates a defect from a preference?

choices.text: Would I have done it differently?
choices.why: That is true of most good changes.

choices.text: Would ignoring it leave the code visibly worse?
choices.why: Right. If not, it is a preference.

choices.text: Is the author junior?
choices.why: The code is the same whoever wrote it.

choices.text: Does the style guide mention it?
choices.why: A guide covers a fraction of choices.

prompt: #31 also changes the heading colour on every page. What should Ana ask?
hint: It may be a good idea; it is a different one.

choices.text: That it move to its own pull request
choices.why: Right. It gets its own review and its own revert.

choices.text: That it be reverted and never tried again
choices.why: The idea may be good; it only belongs elsewhere.

choices.text: Nothing, since the colour looks nice
choices.why: It still changes every page in an ordering pull request.

choices.text: That Bruno explain his taste
choices.why: Taste is not what is wrong; scope is.

prompt: The blocking comment is fixed and only a nit is left. What does Ana do?
hint: A nit is the author's call.

choices.text: Approve and leave the nit
choices.why: Right. Holding it back costs a day and buys little.

choices.text: Wait until the nit is fixed
choices.why: That makes the nit a blocker in disguise.

choices.text: Fix the nit herself on the branch
choices.why: The author decides nits; pushing to their branch takes that away.

choices.text: Close the pull request
choices.why: Nothing is wrong enough for that.

prompt: Why does a slow review cost more than a quick, imperfect one?
hint: What happens to the branch while it waits?

choices.text: Git expires unreviewed branches
choices.why: Git expires nothing of the kind.

choices.text: The branch drifts and the author moves on
choices.why: Right. Coming back costs more each day.

choices.text: Quick reviews are always more accurate
choices.why: Not always; waiting costs more on average.

choices.text: The hosting site closes old pull requests
choices.why: Most do not; the cost is drift and context.

prompt: Which of these belong in Ana's review of #31? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: blocking: an empty time still submits
choices.why: Yes. It is a defect.

choices.text: question: can a customer pick 03:00?
choices.why: Yes. She does not know the answer.

choices.text: I would have used a list of times
choices.why: A preference; both work.

choices.text: Could the colour change be its own pull request?
choices.why: Yes. It is out of scope.

prompt: Which of these are true? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two are about what review is not.

choices.text: New people learn a codebase fastest by reviewing
choices.why: Yes. Reading changes is how the conventions spread.

choices.text: A reviewer should comment on everything they notice
choices.why: Most of what they notice is preference.

choices.text: You can approve and comment at once
choices.why: Yes. Approve with nits.

choices.text: A review is an exam the author passes or fails
choices.why: It is a second reading, not an exam.
